project.title: Digital voltage source, RC response and logic indicators
project.question: How do a digital command and the resulting analog voltage differ in time?
project.notes:
The source exposes both a digital output and explicit 0/5 V terminals. Its voltage charges a 1 kΩ / 1 µF network, whose voltage passes through a Schmitt ADC to a second indicator.

Expected: The direct indicator is HIGH at startup. The RC voltage begins at zero and crosses the 3.5 V high threshold near 1.21 ms with the configured 10 µs maximum step; the sensed indicator then glows red. The capacitor approaches 5 V.

Try: Use Continuous and set DV1 to 0 in Live inputs. Its direct indicator goes LOW immediately; the sensed indicator stays HIGH until the capacitor discharges below 1.5 V. Reducing the maximum step improves numerical convergence.
assumptions: Logic indicators observe resolved 0/1/X/Z events. They add no load or drive strength, and the red glow does not represent LED current or physical brightness.
The displayed state belongs to the selected time and the current project revision. Missing or stale results remain unobserved.
The explicit voltage output is an ideal differential source with finite edges; it has no current limit or output resistance.
The 1 ms RC time constant is solved using coordinated backward Euler; reduce maximum step to check convergence.

annotations.text: The source is HIGH immediately; the RC voltage takes time to cross the ADC threshold.
Continuous → Live inputs: change DV1 to 0, then watch the charged capacitor discharge.

engine.name: CircuitBench coordinated transient
engine.package: CircuitBench stateful MNA and event kernel
engine.execution: Stateful modified nodal analysis and incremental digital events in an isolated worker
engine.coupling: Causal shared timeline; analog trial-step threshold localization; digital events and converter samples create analog breakpoints
engine.limitations: R/C/L and independent V/I sources only in the analog partition. Fixed maximum step with backward-Euler numerical damping; no transistor, diode, opamp, switch, noise or thermal model.

sampling.description: Accepted backward-Euler analog states and settled digital events on one causal timeline. ADC scalar crossing localization is at most 1 ps on the numerical step solution, not a physical-accuracy claim; reduce maximum step for convergence.

bridgeAssumptions: Analog and digital states advance together; digital events, converter sample times, source corners and DAC-ramp ends are solver breakpoints.
One-bit ADCs observe differential voltage without loading. Threshold mode has an X band; Schmitt mode holds its previous known state inside the band.
Multibit ADCs sample at k × period, publish after conversion delay, clip to range and round to the nearest unsigned code. There is no loading, aperture jitter, noise or metastability model.
DACs are ideal finite-edge voltage sources. Multibit DACs hold the configured initial code until the first known word; subsequent X/Z is an error.
The coordinated analog subset is R/C/L and independent V/I sources; backward Euler introduces step-dependent numerical damping.
